review: The game has a weird situation for Turkish players. The game doesn't support Turkish date/time because of that Turkish players can't even see the menu of the game. I did some research and found that this problem is still around here for 2 years and the devs didn't do anything about that but they still sell the game on the steam store for Turkish users.

EDIT: (June 7, 2024): Almost six years later I've come back to give this game another shot along with the DLC and a large suite of mods designed to reduce the tedium and correct many other common annoyances like walk speed and the tiny inventory. I'm generally enjoying it with these mods installed. Unfortunately there's only so much that can be done about the general design of the game, so many of my criticisms in the original review remain, even with mods. So many of the things you unlock are nothing more than stepping stones to other things to unlock. It just starts to feel pointless after a while. Being able to progress faster and not having to juggle inventory every few minutes with the aid of mods makes the game feel far less like a chore, however. 

So if you are looking to buy and play this game as-is, my original review still applies. Some changes have been made since, such as some limited automation with zombies, but they fall well short of fixing the fundamental flaws this game has, in my opinion. If you are willing to install a bunch of mods and play around with their settings to fix some of the game's shortcomings, it may well be worth picking up in a sale.

ORIGINAL REVIEW:

It's been a long time since I found myself this disappointed by a game.

At its core, Graveyard Keeper sounds so appealing. A new and fresh take on the genre with a great theme and more of a focus on structure and progression than its predecessors.

Unfortunately, this is ALL the game is. Progression. Not the satisfying kind, either. It's just progression for its own sake. I noticed before playing the game that many negative reviews mentioned that the game was just "crafting A to get B to get C to get D" and thought to myself "Well, yes. That's what craffting systems ARE". I now know what those people were referring to and that they just did a poor job of articulating their objections. I'll try to explain this criticism: The crafting and progression in this game is going from one means of production to another. From one technology to another. From one material to another. Never really using these new technologies for anything other than a node in a progression chart. Many of them don't need to exist at all. In fact many developers find themselves removing intermediary crafting components throughout the development of the game because they tend to lead to slower and more unsatisfying gameplay and artificial wait times. The fundamental issue here is that almost all of the things you will unlock serve no purpose at all other than to act as a stepping stone to the next unlockable. Your reward for grinding and gathering and crafting is just more of the same with very little new gameplay or systems. There are 3-4 different kinds of wood components (planks, beams, etc). Why? Because they all require different devices to craft (Saw, Table, Chopping block, etc). And each of those devices require multiple components to craft. They serve no purpose other than to pad out the progression and technology tree to make the game appear larger and more complex than it is. This is a problem every system of the game suffers from. Not only do materials take far too long to amass (You can carry only one log after felling a tree, and need to carry it all the way home, then walk all the way back to where you were chopping wood to repeat the process.), but most of the things you use them for only exist as intermediary components of other things. This is usually fine, here and there, but it's ridden throughout the game. 

Let's talk about the grind: It's intense. Frankly, this game has no respect at all for your time. People have mentioned that it often feels like a mobile game with artificial wait times and excessive material requirements. They're right. There's no need for it unless the aim is to artificially pad out the length of the game to give the impression that it has more content than it does. You will find yourself spending multiple days in game, grinding for materials to build or craft a single component in a more complicated recipe, and that recipe is itself only a component of another recipe. This can usually be fine at the start of a game like this: scarecity at the beginning of the game makes progression feel much more rewarding when you're able to obtain many of the same materials much faster after unlocking improved crafting recipes. Only that doesn't happen in Graveyard Keeper. Based on everything I have read and my own experience, if something is scarce or takes a long time to gather or craft or find or process at the start of the game, it's never going to get better or faster, at least not by much. The things you unlock rarely if ever improve your ability to obtain or craft more in less time. So rather than materials becoming easier to stockpile as you progress, they remain tedious to obtain. All the while, your newest recipes and technologies require MORE materials, resulting in a baffling INCREASE in grinding times and a feeling that is entirely opposed to one of progression.

To add to this, there does not appear to be any way to increase the size of your inventory, which will perpetually have half of its space occupied by your tools. Inventory management becomes a nightmare and crafting more and more chests to accommodate your materials makes it tedious to find anything. Your item management never improves. It only gets worse, and given how frustrating it is to farm materials, you are hesitant to part with much, leading to more and more full storage containers.

The game simply lacks quality of life features you would expect in any game of its genre. It's clearly not been playtested thoroughly enough because again, inventory management is another system that becomes more of an annoyance and a step back as you progress in the game. It's the antithesis of satisfaction on the feeling of progression.

Perhaps the biggest and most bizarre flaw in this game is that due to the unreasonable grind, you will only ever spend a fraction of your time dealing with the graveyard or corpses. Most of my time has been chopping wood, gathering stone and building countless devices and apparatus used to process the dozens of smaller components needed to make more of these devices and apparatus. Oh, and waiting for iron ingots to finish smelting. I keep expecting a window to pop up asking me if I want to spend some gems to finish the smelting process faster.

I don't say any of this lightly. I wanted to love this game. I keep trying to love this game. I have quit and re-launched the game many times today hoping that I had just missed something or that a little more time would change my mind, but it only gets worse the more I play. I keep asking myself aloud, "How on earth did they manage to screw this up this badly?" There's just no point to any of it and I can't think of another case where developers have so utterly missed the mark. They have fundamentally misunderstood the appeal of a game like this and don't at all seem to understand what makes a progression sytem fulfilling and entertaining.

There are a number of other significant flaws in the game that have been mentioned by others: An unforgiving energy system, a day/night/week cycle that is meaningless in most ways and a needless bottleneck in others, an apalling lack of communication and information given to the player leading to confusing or aimless gameplay. 

The game certainly doesn't feel finished or tested in the least, but it's the fundamental design philosophy that is far more concerning to me. Will the developers realise where they went wrong or double down? On the bright side, the graphics and music are fantastic, but audio and visuals aren't enough to carry a critically flawed game.

It's possible that Graveyard Keeper can be salvaged, but it's going to take a lot of work and time, and that's only assuming that the developers have the will to stick it out.

It's a real shame.

Does it have flaws? Yep.  Is it grindy?  Sure... if you play it that way.

I think the majority of negativity this game recieves is from people expecting Stardew Valley Dark Edition.  It is not.

What it IS, though, is a challenging, multi-faceted, yet cozy and casual game that you can pick up and play whichever way suits you at the time.   You can micro-manage your time and be super efficient at the cost of a nerve or two... or you can just take your time and do whatever you feel like doing.  The way this game shines to me is that it does not at all feel like it is hurrying me along or pushing me to meet deadlines in-game.   I could spend a week just cutting down trees and making burgers, and I would never feel like "Oh man, I better do all of X or get to Y before Z happens... or else I'll have to wait for next year!!"  

Comfortable.  That's why I like this game.  Even the music is max comfy.

Pros:
- Beautiful, consistent visuals.
- Memorable sound design. 
- Great characters/narrative.
- Satisfying controls.

Combine all that together and you get a truly immersive story.

Cons:
- Restrictive customization, especially with how you lay out your graveyard.
- No character customization, not even clothes/hats.
- There is nothing to do after you complete the base game. No ambient objectives, no big-ticket items to work toward.
- No specialization. You are expected to unlock everything, you only get to pick the order you do it.

Combine all that and you get a game that has zero replay value.

I can't recommend the DLC, and here's why:
- Customization is just as restrictive in the DLC areas.
- There is still very little to work toward. No new big-ticket items. No challenging areas.
- New money-making methods fall flat because of the lack of end-game goals.
- Specialization/decision making is still non-existent.

Graveyard Keeper is a beautiful game that I'm happy I experienced, but I probably won't pick it up again for years, if ever. There's not enough personal attachment because there's so little choice. There's nothing keeping me hooked because I already did everything. DLC just gives me more of the same. 

I'd love to see those issues addressed, but even if they never are I do still recommend this game. The things Graveyard Keeper does right are so excellent that I've felt their absence in every crafting/farm sim I've played since.

I'm not quite sure how this game has such high reviews because it is by far one of the grindiest games I've ever played - so much time is wasted based on completely arbitrary wait times, such as only being able to talk to certain people on certain days. Basically, imagine Stardew valley, but with a much worse map design to force you to walk more, and much, MUCH more grind. And unlike Stardew valley, where unless you're going for a 100% completionist run, you NEED to do everything in a SPECIFIC order in order to advance - you can't put off fishing to the end, for example.
Here's two examples;
The character Snake wants the necronomicon, and says the Astrologer might have it.
Go to the astrologer, who tells you he had a daughter he never knew, with a gypsy woman long ago; he'll give you the book if you help him find out who it is.
So you talk to the gypsy woman's brother, who says he'll help you, if you ask the inquisitor to release a second gypsy woman from prison.
You do, go back, and he tells you it's a woman in town (avoiding name for spoilers).
So you go back to the astrologer, who is excited and asks you to speak to her for him.
You do, she says she never wants to speak to him, and you go back to the astrologer who is distraught.
Finally, he tells you the lighthouse keeper has the book. So you go to him, and he'll give it to you... for five maggots.
Keep in mind that the inquisitor, the astrologer, his daughter, and Snake are only available on certain days, and it'll take you a few weeks to complete this quest; however I skipped over that almost every one of these requires reputation to get a response, to move on. When I did the quest I had the reputation already and could've completed it in a few days if the NPCs didn't decide "Oh I don't feel like being here today."

Example two;
I want to make a body look nice, and for that I need a chemical injection, one of the ingredients is a dark brain. To get one, I need the inquisitor to send me witch corpses.
For that, I need to build a snack stand for his next witch burning, so more people will come.
For that, I need gold star quality beer and burgers.
For that, I need hops, and for hops, I need to repair a mill.
To repair the mill, I need permission to do so, from the millkeeper, and for that, I need to complete Ms. Charm's quest line to the point that she asks me to ask the farmer to let his daughter go with Ms. Charm to the royal court, and the farmer won't let her go unless the mill's repaired.
For Ms. Charm's quest, I need to first get her necklace from Snake, who wants me to get him bloody nails, and 20 skulls for the sacrifice room - and you can't just bloody your own nails no you need to go to level four of the dungeon and kill iron maidens for it.
After that, go to the mountain pass at night and speak to the hunchback, who will tell you he can't get the necklace, so all of this was a waste of time.
Go back to Ms. Charm, who first wants you to get her the perfume of the innkeeper's wife.
For that, you need to deliver some food to the witch, and get a DOZEN FROGS. Lucky, the witch sells them, but only ten at max, and they only slowly restock per day.
After that you get the perfume and give it to Ms. Charm, who will FINALLY give you the quest for the farmer's daughter, that lets you repair the mill, that lets you get the hops for the beer for the inquisitor for the dark brains.
But before all that, you need to get calculations from the astrologer for the mill so I hope you already had good relations with him.
Still following along? Good because this is the entire game, and it wouldn't be so damn bad if EVERY ESSENTIAL CHARACTER WASN'T ONLY AVAILABLE ONE DAY PER WEEK!
So to clarify; I need beer, calculations, perfume and frogs to make the corpses in my graveyard one skull better, but none of what I said are actually in the recipe.
As a final note; the game FORCES you to play a chaotic evil path; you can harvest human flesh to sell for pennies, which I wouldn't mind if it was an option, but several times in the main story line you need human flesh to sell to people to advance the story, with no alternatives. You need to harvest the skulls of 20 corpses in order to progress with the first stage of Snake's quest line, and let me remind you that all the essential NPCs' quests are intertwined so multiple other quests rely on Snake getting this done, so he likes you enough to help you out.
Overall, how is this game rated so highly?

I love this game.  I played through it with a fresh run every time one of the three paid DLCs came out.  Its bugs are numerous, and occasionally game breaking, its dark humor and irreverence are beautiful.  

The game in its base state can be tedious, little to do but follow the story and finish the game, and without a lot of side grinding you won't have a ton of resources or cash by the end.  Its playable, kind of a grind, but fun.

With all its current expacs, its almost too easy.  Participating in the expansions rapidly fills your coffers with cash and prizes, many of which can be used to advance the game without utilizing the whole of your own crafting toolset.  

On yet another hand the game's true "winning" ending requires at least Stranger Sins and Game of Crones, kind of a dick move.  

Better Save Soul is a huge grind, without a payoff beyond being able to harvest and upgrade autopsy parts, and a certain amount of additional automation.  The storyline fizzled  out so suddenly, I went online to find out where to go, only to find out that was it, no closure, expac done.

I find myself with mixed feelings.  I love what this game is at its base, but some of the things it does to get there, and the incomplete state without the first two expansions make it VERY difficult to not see this as a cash grab, selling parts of the game that feel like they should have been in the base game.

I still love this game, and don't regret any of my 180 hours playtime in it, but I hesitated a long time over the "do you recommend this game" buttons.


Oh, one tip for the beginner, don't throw any corpses in the river, make a pile somewhere out of the way until you have the tech to burn them, you need all the ash you can get.

I truly don't understand the negative reviews I'm seeing here. I've played this game all the way through once and halfway through a second time. I had a blast. And on top of that, there are reviews on here that are downright incorrect. For instance, one guy is saying he maxed out his graveyard in a few in-game days. That's literally impossible. Not joking; the way it's set up, you CAN'T max your graveyard until you're about 50 weeks in, at the soonest. The "bug" that stops you from getting corpses is actually a quest in-game, and the reviewers must have gotten confused. It's long (107 hours in, not bored yet), it's fun, it's weird, it looks nice, and the devs fixed a lot of the early issues.

Now that being said, there are a few things you do need to know going in. This game has more crafting stations than I've ever seen in a game. Certain things aren't explained all that well in game. The day system is another example. You WILL need to look at a guide online. And I also recommend watching a few things as you start to figure out how to get blue experience points, getting iron, etc. It starts a bit grindy but once you get food and zombies you can automate almost anything. There are more things but this is just a review, so I'd just say look online.

Look, if you liked Stardew Valley but you're ok with or enjoy having things be a bit darker, you will love this game. I've been a gamer for a long time, and this is one of the few games I've played in the last few years that has that "hook," where I just keep thinking "one more thing, one more thing," and can't seem to quit. (Others: Kerbal Space Program, Subnautica, Stardew Valley of course, Binding of Isaac, Breath of the Wild.) I love it. It's amazing. I hesitated to buy it because of bad reviews, but I shouldn't have. Play the game with the wiki open and you'll have an awesome time.

I don't even really write reviews for games, but seeing all the negative comments for this gem is killing me. This game is a top ten in my Steam library, and I have 205 games. Get it!

TLDR: If you like this kind of game you must play this one with the wiki open. And honestly, that wasn't even enough for me. Usually I ended up googling "How do I get RESOURCE" and getting the answer from Reddit or an article because the fan Wiki is kind of bad. 

I like Graveyard keeper a lot. But this came very close to being a "do not recommend". 

I like the goal of the gameplay loop. I like the way the tech tree works. I absolutely love that you can sleep whenever you want during the day to get your energy back. 

I'm very use to playing games with a wiki open. I have thousands of hours in old school rune scape, a game where it is culturally considered mandatory to read about content on the wiki before trying it so you can get a good gist of what to expect. I use the stardew valley mod that basically puts the wiki in the game. 

Graveyard keeper feels like it knows that players will use wikis and went "Neat, less work for me."

It felt like every time I unlocked a new tool or ability I was frustrated to find out that I need a new surprise resource I've never even heard of to use it. [Looking at you science] And a often times it wasn't anything I had seen referenced or mentioned in game by anyone, meaning I might as well just google "How do I get X" or "How do I make Y" because the game hasn't even given me the smallest hint as to where to start with it. 

So many times I've unlocked an early game progression path only to find out "Don't worry about this. You still have to go unlock 2 other things to use this. See you then." Which just makes you want to hit your head against a wall. I would have just picked to progress those two other paths first if I had known!

I'm going to keep playing. I'm enjoying it, I'll just be defaulting to the wiki a lot sooner instead of trying to figure out anything in game myself to be honest, which does take a little of the magic out of it.

It's great if you love repetition and slowly automating everything. I do feel like a lot of it isn't needed. I never really saw a point to fish for example. I love it when the game is a Re-Animator style mad scientist simulator and not Stardew Valley.

I came across this game as I was browsing my recommended feed on Steam, and since it seemed like a charming, if a little morbid, "farming simulator" style game I picked it up on a winter sale. While I certainly enjoyed it for a little while with its cute art style and the interesting game mechanic of managing a graveyard, there are several things that detracted from my gameplay experience and make me hesitant to replay now that I have wrapped up the main story. I'll break down the big things that I really liked, and the things that I think turned into the downfalls of this game:

Pros:
[olist]
[*] Graphics - As with most indie games these days, this game has a charming pixelated art style that also offers quite a bit of detail that is really pretty to look at no matter how long you play. Especially with the seemingly random changes in the weather - the rainy evenings and foggy mornings are always a breath of fresh air to see!
[*] Graveyard Concept - I don't know why, but the idea of managing a graveyard was such an interesting concept that it made me want to pick it up more, despite the more morbid undertones that come with the idea. The mechanics behind managing your own graveyard turned out to be sound and well thought out, [spoiler]There's a whole scoring system for the "quality" of a corpse that can be changed with autopsies and embalming in order to get a well prepared body for burial.[/spoiler] The whole system of the graveyard itself was really enjoyable, and I for one hardly got tired of partaking in this part of the game.
[*] NPC interactions - The NPC's that you encounter as your friends and givers-of-quests are all charming and well thought out with how they interact with your character and with their relationships with each other. In the world of The Graveyard Keeper, each NPC has had some interaction of some sort with other NPC's, and it shows in their questlines and background stories. However, while I greatly enjoyed this feature, it was not a super prevalent part of the game that and I genuinely wish it was a bigger feature.
[/olist]
Cons:
[olist]
[*] The Grind - The biggest thing that I found detracted from the gameplay experience was the Grind you had to go through to acquire certain items or complete certain tasks. Now, I should clarify that I enjoy games that I can collect stuff in - Minecraft and Stardew Valley being at the top of the list in that category - so I thought that I could handle the extensive collecting I read about in other reviews of this game. Oh how I was wrong. Well, at first I was alright, because in the start there are only a few things that demand you to constantly collect things for - things like wood and stone for instance. However, as you continue to unlock new things and the quests become more resource demanding, you start to feel the sting of "The Grind". This feeling is compounded even more by the infuriatingly small energy bar. Which you must either replenish with food (that you need to grind for) or sleep and waste precious time. While this is certainly helped by the game's new Zombie update, it feels like the benefits of that update only kick in during the later half of the game, and only if you dedicate more time and resources into creating those automated systems.
[*] Energy Usage - As stated in the point above, there is a painfully small energy bar that dictates how much you can accomplish during a given time. The only way to remedy this is to consume an unbelievable amount of food or to sleep, which makes in-game time pass quickly. While about 10 hours in, you can establish a farm and grow a good supply of food, the demand to keep making and gathering food to support such an easy to consume resource is just too unbalanced in my personal opinion. I feel if there could be upgrades available to expand your energy bar or to make it so that you need to sleep less/lessen sleep deprivation effects, it would be more fun, especially in the later parts of the game.
[*] Closed off Areas - Somewhere between 5 and 15 hours into the story, you will come across some quests from some NPC's that refer to other areas in the game that sound like places you can travel to in order to expedite their given quests. [spoiler]I'm referring to the Town, a rather often mentioned place within the story of the game[/spoiler]. However, upon trying to get to said areas, you are either immediately killed (don't worry, death isn't a threat in this game) or are permanently blocked out by another NPC. There are no future quests you can complete or items you can acquire to get around these blockages, and personally I found it to be quite misleading and disappointing. It just makes it feel like the game isn't complete yet, despite being fully released for many months now.
[*] Endgame - While I certainly had fun during the first third of the game, collecting things and completing quests. The late game quests and stories feel like they were more of a chore to complete, and with very little payoff. This is partly due to The Grind, but also because of a combination of time management the direction the story took. When I say "time management", I am referring to how this game makes you wait in order for end game quests to be completed. For example: [spoiler]As you wrap up the last quests with the Astrologer and Ms. Charm, you are require to wait until the following in-game week to progress their questlines [/spoiler]. This would not be a problem if there was still other things to do and accomplish, but at this point you already have all the upgrades you need, and most of the other quests have already wrapped themselves up. You simply must putz around grinding some more as you wait for the clock to tick by. And as for the story...[spoiler]It is a rather short ending that feels kind of patched together and thrown in at the last second. This is more so because of the last cutscene regarding Donkey and Gerry the skull joking about this game being a ploy for DLCs[/spoiler]. I feel like the story had so many opportunities to be deeper, but it very much missed the opportunity to be in pursuit of letting you chop and mine and craft all the things.
[/olist]

Overall, while the idea of managing a graveyard was a draw in-and-of-itself, there was not as much graveyard managing as I would have liked, and instead there was more than enough grinding of resources, an incomplete-feeling world, and a lack-luster story. If you are looking at this game interested in the concept, I implore you to [b]really[/b] consider how much of "The Grind" you can take, because I thought I could handle it, and I greatly overestimated myself. If you can tolerate the gathering part of the game, then I am certain you will have a good time with this game. However, I personally do not recommend it if you don't think you can put up with the gathering, as that is the great majority of the gameplay.

This is a slightly tough one to recommend. I can't deny playing it somewhat obsessively, but I don't know that I can say I have a ton of fond memories for playing it. Short of the very end of the game, when some automation starts taking off, there is just always so, so, so much that needs to be getting done at any moment. And it's not in the Stardew Valley way, where you'll get to it tomorrow. It's just always piling up, more and more to do, and some of it has to happen on certain days of the in game week, and it's just a lot to keep track of and do. It doesn't encourage healthy gameplay.

The game is also very bleak. From helping burn witches, to helping neighbors do bad things to each other because they hate each other, you'll be forced into doing a lot of bad things if you want to progress the plot. Not even bad for the greater good, but just being rotten.

It's not the break I was looking for from a sometimes bleak and overworked life. I hoped it would paid off, but it really didn't.

But the gameplay is fairly solid, so I'm sure it's the right game for some people. Complements to the devs for making your basic tools not take up valuable inventory slots, and for using the E and F keys to "do" rather than endlessly having to switch between the right tools. 

The depth of the trees for upgrading what you can do is really good, and the barriers to getting to the next part of it seem really well thought out. It's a pain to work around, but one that's pushes that Fun button every time you figure out how to get the points you need. 

Crafting is really neat, and the ability to automate it later is a huge boon. 

The fact that they block you from getting too rich too fast could be annoying, but I think is a good mechanic in the end. It keeps prices from having to ascend into the millions of gold pieces to keep up with what you're bringing in.

While I complain about the schedule with some people only being available once a week, it does keep the town fresh, with specific things that you can only do that day.

It's a good game, with solid design and a lot of plot in it. It wasn't really for me, but I think it's worth a try.

Addicting. Certainly not for everyone (but definitely for me). In my first 20 hours of play I finally found that feeling again of playing Stardew Valley for the first time. I continued to enjoy my next 45 hours in this capitalist purgatory and expect to continue twiddling away. 

On the negative side, this seems like a corporation's response to Stardew Valley. It seems partially thought-out, has scope creep, and is missing some heart. It is clear when so many little things are off - inventory management problems (many glaring but also batch-moves are inconsistent), translation, pause, inconsistent animations (why does the Bishop still use the mirror he gave me?), and annoying crafting inconsistencies. 

There was a nice effort in putting this game together and it has even more potential, along with these and other several issues. There are a decent number of funny moments but I feel like there could have been more too.

Update after finishing the game :

Still wouldn't recommend it. 
I was at 34 hours of gameplay, and it took me basically an extra 30 to finish the game from where i was at. I will say that what brought me to replay the game was the Dev,s reply i received months ago, but even with the zombie mechanic, that thank god helps shave off SOME grind... i'd easily add 5 to 10 hours of menial running between the quarry and the house, i cannot say the game felt any better.

Some major flaws tend to show themselves towards the last quarter of the game that feels like a way to extend the duration of the game (padding)  

- Quests go on for ages. 
Stuff like delivering an item to someone then being forced to wait a full in game week before being able to complete the next step of the quest even if you already have the items you need. Or being sent to talk to one NPC to make a tiny step towards the next quest which also takes days. 

- The money system
You basically face a quest that takes "about" 12 weeks (about 1 gold a week) to complete and that is if you manage to get decent enough money from the veggie company. 
Yes, you can earn a little extra ont he side ( crafting some late game items, Sunday masses, etc) but even with over 300 graveyard rating and 80+ faith i barely got more than 22 silver a week from mass. 

- The combat system / Dungeoning
Little to no variety in monsters. Most floors will have Slimes, Bats and Flies. 
Then from 5th floor you'll find tiny metal men, and way beyond that (aroudn 10th floor) you'll get black range attacking slimes, spiders, and elementals. That's it.
There's also 0 feedback when you get hit and i've seen my life drain extremely fast at times with a bat just "spazzing" out next to me.

34 hours in and it feels like double that.

I'd like to say a few things about this fun little game.  I usually like to play a game and then go check out the negative reviews.  Most of the people usually complain about the same things. 

Things to note about this game.  

1.  It's not Stardew Valley, for the love of all that is holly please stop referring to Stardew Valley all the time.  PLEASE DO NOT TREAT THIS GAME LIKE STARDEW VALLEY.  ITS NOT!!

2. It's not a factory, production line, grinding to level up etc. game.  It can mistakenly come across, at first glance, as one.   I played like more than 30 hours of the game before going “is it me or is this going nowhere”.  Then I took the time to look up the game and see how veterans play it. 

The problem with these two above expectations is that:

A) you're going to be disappointed at the "farming" as it's not a farming game.  It has farming in it, but its NOT a farming game.  No relation to any farming sim out there at all.

B) you're going to grind and grind and grind and 40 hours later wonder why you're alive, and wonder if continued existence is really wroth it.  The answer is obviously no because you've missed the point entirely. So Don't Get Trapped By The Belief That You Must Grind.  Make what you need as and when you need it.

This game teaches you what the game is actually about from the outset.  Make grave yard pretty.  Oh ok.  Then the very next thing you get is a dead body.  Butcher dead body for parts, put in grave, make grave pretty.  Unlock church with pretty graveyard.  Preach to people who pay you money and faith. "DUN-DUHHH" THE POINT of the game.  Make gorgeous bodies (alchemy late game), to put into gorgeous graves (marble carvings late game), to preach to people in a gorgeous church (final upgrade late game).  THIS IS THE POINT OF THE GAME.

Everything else is for fun. HAVE FUN.  There is no point to the game other than being an excellent graveyard keeper.  

Grinding, who cares.  You've got 2 zombies each at the stone, marble and mining sites.  A zombie at the wood yard, porter zombies bring the stone, iron, coal, wood, etc from the quarry and wood yard.  Zombies working for all eternity on the farms, zombies at the work stations mass producing items.  Your job is to put in orders for stuff and dabble in alchemy, which lets you make beautiful bodies and get tons of money from your sermons because you've a gorgeous graveyard and an impressive church.  

In the 25 odd years I've been playing RPG games I've NEVER, not once, found a fetch and carry quest "worth it's weight in salt".  So please, weak complaint get over it.  It's an RPG staple.  The end.  All quests lead to something.  In this game, if you think its fame and glory, you're going to be gravely disappointed.  In this game it leads to unlocking things.  You have to use what you've unlocked to make you rich, or at least useful.  Unlocking things quickly will let you get on with the actual game faster.  So don't waste time grinding thinking that that's how you make money.  Selling stuff at the various merchants is going to backfire, because that's not the mechanics of this game and a lot of the stuff you can make, you can't sell.  So, you'll just end up having a lot of stuff you can't sell, and tons of it, because you mistakenly believed that you had to grind.  If you've unlocked it, move on.  Only make what you need, nothing more.

This game has a dungeon and “battle system” [spacebar].  If you think the battles are fun but bemoan a dungeon where you can engage in that fun more extensively, you need to re-think why you're complaining (or even alive)?  There is nothing wrong with changing things up.  Don't use Stardew Valley as an excuse to justify your complaints either.  I found the dungeon a nice change of pace after 40 hours of game play and 155 bread rolls later.  

As you unlock relations with various characters, you'll make money selling those veggies you though were useless because you're selling them raw to the farmer, and not packaged to the trader.  You'll make tones of money selling quality produce at a tent every Wrathday burning witches at the stake.  You'll be selling quality booze at your pub and a few other weekly staple sources of actual income as you progress.  These are not the purpose of the game, just extras.  The money will come.  Unlocking production lines and skill trees and various levels is easy, and not the point.  

If you think the game is about the story, it isn't.  If you think its about the quests, it isn't.  If you think its about the farming, the grinding, the one and only dungeon, the fishing, the cooking, the harvesting, the crafting, It ISN"T.  

It's about dicking around here and there and everywhere, doing little bits of this and that, whilst building a kick ass church and graveyard, because the game is called graveyard keeper, and then having snorts and giggles at the creators poking fun at controversial elements of human debauchery.  There is no deep meaningful purpose to the existence of the Graveyard Keeper other than to have some fun doing a little bit of everything.  You don't specifically have to focus on any one single thing.  You can do something and then do something else afterwords.  You don't even have to finish the first thing you were busy with.  There is no rush, no time limits to anything.  

There is no realism, no Oscar nominating writing.  It's just a silly little game, with silly little antics and a “F*%@” ton of stuff to do.  If that isn't your cup of tea, so be it.  Go find some game that has “realism” to it and deep satisfying meaning where you can be as serious as you want to be.  Me I play games to loose the realism and shed those tedious layers of seriousness.  

Peace out and find a sense of humour (life is hard without one).

I really wanna love this game, but it's stressful for me to play. It doesn't explain even remotely as much as it should. I have to tab out and Google something so often, it's hard to enjoy playing it. There just needs to be more information readily available in-game. There are also some irritating things about placement. You should be able to move things around. If you place something right next to the well, you can't walk around it and it acts funky when you try to use it. One of my zombies also disappeared when I tried to place him there for work. Definitely seems like an unpolished game. Like it should be in early access still. I don't like that the quest information is so minimal and as vague as it can possibly be, and for some reason, grouped with the NPC tab. I don't understand that at all. I'll have to Google every quest in the game just to remember or figure out what it needs because all it says is something like, "Help the witch with her memory". Okay?? Help me with mine! lol!

I had to spend some time thinking about this after finishing the game. Admittedly I was torn between a positive or a negative review. Ultimately after reflecting I realized this game left me disappointed at best and frustrated at worst.

[h1]Crafting[/h1]
Nothing is really explained how to craft anywhere. Whats worse: is you have like 30 workbenches to navigate between. The tech tree might show you what workbench an item is crafted at for some things but then theres no indication of where you can build workbenches at all (so youre going to each area to see 'can I build it here'). Some items are only obtainable by using alchemy, where some recipes are never shown to you. I get that this game is meant to be a 'discover on your own' but this game is unnecessarily convoluted in many ways so discovering some things is statistically unlikely to accidentally discover. Whats worse: some items you do discover you can craft are never shown to you again (i.e. such as the mixing table) so you better have something next to your computer to write it down! To make matters even worse still: some items are not craftable at all. I go through all of this to tell you that you spend a lot of time walking between workbenches completely frustrated, trying to figure out how to craft something, only to end up at google and figure out you cant craft it at all and must be bought from vendor A, and can only be bought after doing X, Y, and Z.

On a semi-related point, there is absolutely no f'in reason for there to be as many crafting benches in a game like this. I get that a hammer and a sandwich arent crafted from the same place but why does there need to be a distinction between types of wood working benches? This isnt a 10/10 realistic living simulator. Put it all in the same workbench like the super-retro-arcade-RPG that this is.

[h1]Vendors UI[/h1]
Same is true for vendors. You cant really see what vendors sell until you unlock their final level. Since some quests are locked behind some vendors, this can get old fast. Again, google becomes the game; clearly not the thing youre supposed to do but its the only way to figure out some of this stuff (in a reasonable amount of time).

[h1]Quests[/h1]
Quests are more of the same. There is no quest panel like in a normal RPG. Instead, the quest panel is merged with the NPC panel list. At best its not intuitive and at worst it absolutely doesnt work at all. So to jump straight to the 'worst', some quests are not directly associated with an NPC. Meaning some quests are completely invisible after theyve been assigned to you. So if you talk to an NPC right before youre shutting off your computer for the night and you werent paying close attention to what they said; you might play the game again in 3 or 4 days and not remember what the hell youre supposed to do. Again, google, and again, clearly no game is meant to be played through google; least of all a single player game.

Despite my best effort to try to immerse myself and enjoy the game via the narrative and trying to learn game mechanics organically through the same narration, I just couldnt. Some things are so poorly explained, some things are not explained at all, and some things you just end up forgetting about because there is no proper quest or proper crafting panel.

[h1]Items[/h1]
The reason to craft anything is: N/A. I spent the entire first 1/3rd of this game thinking 'this is like Stardew Valley with a graveyard'. It wasnt until later that I realized that this isnt even 1/3rd of the game Stardew Valley is; its a lame knockoff with a grungy aesthetic. Trying to immerse myself into the game organically (without google) and thinking this was SV, I tried optimizing my graveyard and home area for output. You realize real quick that there is absolutely no reason to grow or craft most of the things in the game. WHY EVEN HAVE IT IN THE GAME IF YOU CANT USE IT?

I didnt understand how the economy worked early in the game (avoiding google) so I grew a bunch of hemp because I thought I could sell the hemp and use the seeds for oil. Only to find out that you cant sell it or use hemp for anything but candles (worthless; only used for sermons but those are also pointless). Not to mention the economy of this game is absolute trash anyway so you end up with more money than you know what to do with and you can buy all the oil you ever need.

This isnt an isolated incident either. Lots of items in the game are like that. In fact, the kitchen workbench I practically never used outside of quests that forced me to use it. You end up having to google 'what can I sell, where and at what vendor level' because the game is needlessly uninformative to this end. In a normal RPG you just sell anything to anyone. I get in real life that I cant walk up to my car mechanic and sell him a tomato, but this is a f'in arcade game isnt it? Lets treat it that way.

But its worse. Some things you would expect vendors to buy; they just wont. Gold Beer you would expect to be sold at the tavern. The barkeep takes bronze and silver beer but will not buy gold beer. Something like Gold Wine can be sold in the base game (once a week) but to really make gold you find out you need the Stranger Sins DLC. UGH. Boring. Just let me sell it at the tavern where people drink. FFS.

[h1]Story[/h1]
Really, theres no reason to do anything at all outside of the story. And I mean that in the literal sense. This is a strong difference to other RPGs where there are other things to do outside of the story that are just fun to do or otherwise aide your progression of the story. This game has almost zero of that (except creating zombies and micromanaging the small amount of goods you can sell to vendors).

Theres even a dungeon (just like SV) but I found myself bored with it about 16 levels in and realized there was nothing to keep me going down there. So I stopped. My gameplay didnt change at all, nor would it have if I would have continued. Youre really only required to go to level 3 or 4 to craft an item you need for a quest.

Even in the credits that roll after a lackluster story and ending, they f'in joke about "but we didnt [spoiler]go to the town[/spoiler] or [spoiler]see the ship[/spoiler]", "Ah the developers will just make a DLC to make people find out that stuff! Ha Ha!" Are you f'in kidding me? So you consciously knew your story and game was bad and now youre making fun of your customers for falling for it? F'in attrocious.

[h1]Game Pace[/h1]
Wow its bad. Sometimes youre rushing around trying to do 15 things at once and sometimes youre sitting there with nothing really to do at all, waiting for 3 or 4 days to pass. It became apparent fast that the culprit is the day-cycle. Unlike other RPG games that have seasons, this game has days. You might imagine that allows you a faster interval around things to do during different periods but its far worse. Instead, there is such a limited amount of time you have to do X, Y and Z, maybe you only have enough time to get X in.

Some quests need you to deliver X on a day, so you wait for them in front of their house as the sun comes up to give it to them. Then they hit you right back with a 'give me Y' and you have to rush to get the materials, craft and bring it back before the sun goes down. Half the time I was missing something or didnt make Y before sunset so you have to wait a whole extra week for that day to come back to finish the delivery.

This whole mechanic just felt unnecessary and just made the pacing of the game way too fast at some times and way too slow at others.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
At the end of the day, I played the game a bit. And I thought I enjoyed it; but after reflecting on what I did in the game and why, I enjoyed it because I thought I was working towards something. When the game ended and I realized, "Oh, that was it!?!?", that's when I ended up realizing this game wasn't good; it's just a busy-work simulator masquerading as an RPG.

The game is one of those games that is more addictive than fun. The level of grind is pretty hardcore. The days are quite short, further exacerbated by the fact that you can empty out your stamina bar in about a minute depending on the activity, requiring you to sleep or craft food to regenerate it. 

The game has its flaws. Much of the information required to progress in the game is simply not there and requires you to look it up to figure things out. There is no quest journal to remind you what you need to do to accomplish your goal. Rarely will the NPC remind you how to do the task you were given hours ago. The whole process of alchemy doesn't have any in-game tutorial. There are hundreds of combinations and no hint for what you need to use to get something even as simple as paper ink. (EDIT: There was an update to the game right after my review that gives you hints for alchemy recipes. Props for that. The updates to the game are encouraging.)

The crafting trees you have to go through to get one thing can get very excessive. It's not uncommon to have to go through several processing stations to craft one thing you want. Each step taking up a sizeable chunk of your stamina bar, requiring you to sleep again and again, processing and processing and processing every single day hundreds of times. That's the bulk of the gameplay. Just..processing everything. If that's fun for you, knock yourself out.

The game has a lot of good traits. The music was pleasing to hear even after many hours. The writing, what little there is of it, is charming. The artstyle is excellent. But it just lacked the core of what any game needs, FUN. Progression is slow and it is tedious. There's little room for creativity because everything takes such an elongated, drawn out process to build, and you lose materials to tear something down if you want to move it. What areas you are allowed to build in, aren't very big. You'll get a big area, but are only allowed to build in sections of that area. There's a ton of grind, for very little reward. The game doesn't get more fun as you go. You just unlock more machines to process more things.

The 93% positive reviews on Steam are deceptive. If you read even the positive reviews, you will see people admitting just how grindy it is.Ultimately you get many hours for $20, IF YOU CAN GET INTO IT. That's the question. So possibly a lot of bang for your buck. Now whether or not you'll be having fun doing it? Really depends on how much free time you have to grind. Like I said, more addictive than fun. People play grind heavy MMOs, but are they really having fun doing that? (As a former MMO player myself, I can safely say NO. The fun comes from the interactivity and competing with others, which isn't in this game.) Just keep that in mind. There are games out there that have FUN and not endless tedious work, or at least give equivalent returns for the effort.

Speaking of which, your money is better spent on Terraria or Stardew Valley. Terraria is $10, SDV is $15. Both cheaper than this game with better reviews, way more content, multiplayer, and without a soul crushing grind. The only reason you see high gameplay times for people from this game is because of how grindy it is. For the former two games, it's because they're actually content heavy. Now if the grind and processing lessened up, rewards for tasks increased to a level where they matched the effort involved, and if there was some CREATIVE OUTLET in this game, I can see it being good. SDV you can beautify your farm, Terraria you can build a beautiful palace. The creative avenues in this game are very restrictive by comparison. 

Fix these issues, and I'll come back to it. I feel like there is a lot of potential here, because the things you can craft look quite nice. Having more creative freedom would go a long way. Also adding multiplayer would alleviate quite a bit of the grind, and make it more fun, without changing the core gameplay.

TL;DR
Has the grind of an MMO without the interactivity and the player competition an MMO does. Not enough reward for the amount of effort involved in daily tasks.
The bulk of the gameplay is processing things endlessly. 
Very little room to be creative because of how long it takes to build anything, and tearing things down doesn't give you everything back. There's not much room to build wherever you want to.
Is in dire need of a quest journal with at least vague hints of how to do something.
SDV ($15) and Terraria ($10) are cheaper than this ($20) with way more content, plus multiplayer, plus fun, minus excessive, unrewarding grinding. But with updates, this game stands a solid chance. They would just have to be quite drastic. Multiplayer is not easy to implement from my understanding.

Graveyard keeper is an amazing game full of great content! I usually read negative reviews before buying games so I was worried about buying this game, but this is one of the cases were the negative reviews are either empty or entirely preference based so I'm glad I bought the game and gave it a try. 

A big negative comment from people is that there is too much walking. I don't actually find the walking a problem at all. I enjoy walking places, and on the way you can pick up resources or do other tasks. The in game music is great and also helps the walk be more enjoyable. There are fairly good shortcuts and more shortcuts get unlocked as you play. That being said, god forbid there's a game where you actually have to play the game... and walk places... as opposed to just magically teleporting everywhere. You forget a nail when you walked across the map to build something? Who cares? It's not that big of a deal that I forgot a nail so now I need to give the game a negative review. My god. 

The other complaint is that the crafting system is too complex and too grindy. It's actually not that grindy for a player who is a completionist. I love completing things. Give me more things to do, and that's just more things to complete and I love seeing the progression over time. Yes progression is slow but guess what? It's not a demanding game, Graveyard Keeper is actually a casual game. There are no deadlines, no time limits, unlike star dew valley where you need to do everything in a period of 3 years and you can miss content, and so you really need to study the wiki and know the in game calendar so you don't miss talking to people. In Graveyard Keeper you can play 1000 days and just farm apples the whole time if you wanted, with 50 chests full of apples. There is no demand to complete or do anything in any order at any time before any dates which for me makes the game less stressful than Stardew Valley was. An example of a complex game is Factorio, which was so complex it was mind boggling and boring at times and I had to return that game immediately (even though it's probably a good game just not my style). But Graveyard Keeper? I don't call this complex, I call this interesting content.

Another complaint in negative reviews is that the game is too hard and you don't know what to do. I also have to disagree with this. The amount of time I've played games where I was reading the wiki 50% of the time was a lot. And I still enjoyed those games, so if that was the case with Graveyard Keeper I would admit it and still probably enjoy it. But, I actually didn't have to look up much after 36 hours of gameplay. Most of it you figure out, if you get stuck just move on to something else, and then maybe later something you unlock ties into the other thing you were stuck on and it all makes sense after. If you just enjoy the game, try not to be fixated on 1 task and treat the game more sandbox casual you will start to love it and find that you don't need the wiki for much. Also the wiki is really well put together. I've played games with horrendous wiki's that were confusing and or missing content. 

The talking to people on specific days is not a problem. It took me awhile to figure this out but each day corresponds to 1 specific person, and the colour of that day matches that persons clothing colour, so once you realize this it's very easy to remember what days you can talk to who. Need the astrologer? Well the astrologer wears blue and the only blue day is the day with the moon symbol. Just like the merchant wears orange/brown and the orange brown day is called greed. etc. All very easy to keep track of. 

Most complaints on this game people should be ashamed of for a game that goes on sale for $5.... this is an amazing steal with hours and hours of content at $5. You should definitely consider buying this game when it's on sale! And I would argue it's even worth it's regular price.

I loved the first 100 days of gameplay I spent on this title, which amounts to quite a few hours, but as a developer myself, I honestly cannot recommend it in its current state. Graveyard Keeper has that "Stardew Valley but Metal" charm, but it’s notorious for what we call "obfuscated design." It’s a game of nested dependencies, where to get A, you need B, but B requires C, and the game refuses to give you the recipe for C until you've already found it. I'm sure some people enjoy it but it's far from the vast majority

The game could be incredibly fun, but as many have pointed out, it is an absolute chore to navigate without constantly checking Google or the wiki to figure out what you are actually supposed to do next. Setting aside the grind (which I was warned about), you spend at least one-third of the early game sleeping because you can’t consistently cook decent food. The energy pool should easily be twice its current size; the only reason I can think of for it being this small is to artificially inflate the game's length, making it seem like you’re being productive when you aren't.

While energy issues and the grind can be mitigated late-game through cooking and automation, I estimate that the vast majority of players quit before reaching that point. Energy management needs to be far more efficient, and playing without a proper quest guide makes the experience incredibly frustrating. For example, if you desperately need Blue Tech early on, good luck figuring out that you need to study specific body parts, and it sucks to be you if you don't eat Cake beforehand, as that's a one-time study bonus.

Early-game money-making is an absolute slog. If you want Pen and Ink, it’s better to craft them yourself by mid-game, but the process is a circular nightmare: To get Pen and Ink, you need Ink and Feathers. Feathers can’t be crafted or gathered; they must be purchased from the Astrologer or found in the Egg Basket. To get Ink, you need Black Paint, which is discovered through trial-and-error at the Alchemy Workbench. Eventually, you might realize you can make it from Graphite Powder and Water, but to get Graphite Powder, you have to study Graphite at the Study Table to realize it can even be fed into the Alchemy Mill.

You see where I'm going with this...? The game provides zero hints for any of these steps.

Overall, the game starts strong and develops in a silly, charming way. The map is well-designed and the developer's passion is evident, but certain elements absolutely need to change:

• A functional quest log: The current system is far too vague.
• A more efficient energy system: A larger pool and faster rest cycles.
• Reduced early-game grind: This would be largely solved by the energy fixes.
• Building mobility: The inability to move structures is baffling. Disassembling and reassembling already costs energy but on top of that, it only returns half the materials. In the early game, losing rare materials this way can literally lock you out of content for hours.

While mods can fix some of these issues, the core experience requires alt-tabbing every two minutes to figure out your next move. Otherwise, you’re forced to keep manual notes on NPC inventories (which change throughout the game) and grind for hours just to process basic resources.

Minor QoL Suggestions:

• An eastern entrance for the Church. (Easily doable)
• A mount or sprint mechanic to double movement speed.
• More shortcuts in the underground tunnels that don't make them seem like traveling through IKEA.

With these changes, I would give this game a top rating. In its current state, however, it becomes a chore long before it becomes fun. As an average user, I would honestly give it a positive, because double digit hours of fun for a game makes it worth it, but as a fellow dev, my critique is probably much more helpful than an additional thumbs up would be.

Graveyard Keeper is top-down management game like Harvest Moon or Stardew Valley, but with a macabre twist. Sadly, this game is on the cusp of being great but is currently bogged down by lack of polish.

The game currently suffers from:
-Your main character lacking a sprint ability.
-Combat being terrible and lacks feedback. Enemies simply phase through you and you lose health.
-You can't move placed workbenches/objects even after you you've built them and increased your yard space.
-Certain tasks require way too much time, looking at you Red Jello.
-Whetstones need to have their cost halfed, because without one your game will reach a bottleneck.
-Tutorials are obtuse and need improvement. Morever, quest-givers should always drop a hint as to were to go, looking at you Donkey and wheel grease.
-On the topic of quests, every quest should yield some small reward because some smileys feel like a real waste. Especially after spending 2 silvers on Wine, looking at you Gerry.
-You can't look up blueprints in your tech tree, so you have to constantly run to a buidling station and write it down.
-Your chests aren't connected across the board, so be prepared to make a system.
-Half of your inventory will be stuffed with tools. Please make a toolbelt. Furthermore, Faith and Sermons should just be in your inventory like gold and should not take up a full space.
-Missing sound effects, prepare to experience the quietest downpour ever.
-Pacing is poor and the game is marred by increasingly sisyphean tasks.

Bottom Line:
Graveyard Keeper is not a bad game but it was not ready to be released out of Early Access. The devs do deserve praise though as they have been busting their asses to update the game post-release. In fact, my complaint of days being too short has already been rectified. Hopefully, they keep on steering the game in the right direction.

Graveyard Keeper is a pretty good game that can best be compared to stardew. That is how I bought it. I enjoyed stardew, wanted something similar, found this game and tried it.

Let me start by stating some really important things about the game : 

YOU WILL NEED THE WIKI OPEN. 

I see tons of reviews of people who got stuck because they didn't know what to do next. This game contains very little direction in terms of what to do. You might need an item for a quest, and the only way to get said item is some hidden NPC selling it and the game will never tell you. We can argue wether or not this is a flaw of the game, but if you plan on playing it, don't make the same mistake other players did. I myself tried to do it on my own and fared pretty well for a while, but about 10 hours in had to give up and look up some things on the wiki.

THIS GAME IS SIMILAR TO STARDEW VALLEY, BUT NOT THE SAME

The basic concept is the same. You have a plot of land on which you can do quite a few things, there is a town with npcs you can interact with, the overall ambiance is relaxed and warm. You have "chores" to do to progress in a multitude of ways. There are some objectives, but at the end of the day you could just stay in your spot and do whatever you want. No pressure or stress to complete any kind of objective.

The difference with stardew is the progression. In this game, the primary means of progression is through a tech tree. Through certain actions of certain nature, you unlock specific science points that allow you to unlock technologies to unlock new items or crafting stations. These items you ear are usually needed for quests or quality of life improvements.

The npc system, in my eyes, is actually better than stardew's. In this game, most npcs have quests for you that are part of a bigger storyline, and when you complete a quest for an npc you earn reputation with them, allowing you acces to certain services or dialogue options. This feels far more interactive and fun than stardew's friendship system. This is , in my mind, probably one of the only thing this game does better than stardew.

If you liked stardew valley, there is a decent chance you will enjoy this game. They are similar, but have some fundamental differences.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Now let's talk about the game itself. You start off as a regular guy who dies and goes into some strange other dimension and become a graveyard keeper. There is a graveyard, and a steady flow of bodies to the graveyard, your job is to embalm them and bury them, burn them, throw them in a river, whatever. That is the basic premise.

A part from this, the main underlying quest is our character wants to go back to the real world, and every npc you meet usually gives you quests when you ask them for help. Those quests usually require you bringing them items or accomplishing something.

The quest system is pretty fun. You meet npcs, they give you quests, and you try and work to complete them. What is nice is a lot of npcs tend to get intertwined with other npc's quest lines and I just find it overall fun and interactive.

This is where we get to the main feature of this game : the tech tree. Your actions in the world earn you tech points that allow you to learn new technologies. These technologies are usually to make you stronger, more efficient at certain tasks, or allow you to create new crafting stations or items that can be required for certain quests. The tech tree makes this game, "complex", for lack of a better word. Often you'll need a technology for a quest, but then you will need another technology to use that technology, and you need another technology for that one, and so on and so forth. You can find yourself in some pretty deep rabbit holes sometimes in terms of what you need to do. Personally, I love problem solving and therefore this part of the game, but it isn't for everyone.

The game includes things such as fishing, farming, mining, combat and so on. Later in the game there is the ability to automate certain tasks and make your life far easier.

The overall tone of the game is a curious one. Not in a bad way, just special. At it's core it's pretty macabre, you bury bodies that you often remove chunk from prior to burying them. You can take out from the body and make a burger with it, or sell it at the bar with an illegal royal stamp so it looks legit. Anyone analysing this kinda feels like this is messed up. However, it's all presented in a light hearted funny tone with nothing being graphically explicit. Personally, I love this tone, but some people might find it strange and unamusing.

The graphics are great. They are nice looking for 2d sprites with nothing groundbreaking.

The game has two big issues for me. First of all, the mandatory use of the wiki. Pretty much everyone who doesn't use the wiki will get stuck and uninstall the game. USE THE WIKI. I personally don't mind this, but some people might.

The biggest issue in my mind is the price tag. This game, at it's current default price, is in my eyes too expensive to justify buying. It's good, but not that good.

The game currently sits at 20 USD. To me this game is probably worth, at the most, 13-15 USD and 20 is kind of pushing it. I was able to get it at a 65% discount for a price of 6.7 USD and for that price it is a complete steal.

TL:DR : This game is pretty great but too pricey. I recommend getting it if the price falls below 15 USD

It's a pretty game, with compelling mechanics and sense of progression, multiple levels of complexity and interconnectiveness between different parts, and apparently a good story to boot. It makes you explore the world and the mechanics to solve the problems.

However, it's just a multi-dimensional game of solitaire. You can only do A once you've researched technology B, which requires having already completed quest C, which requires making item D, which is made at a crafting station that requires you make component E, which requires researching technology F, which requires you to collect a pile of coloured tech points, one of which then requires you to 'study' items using faith, which is in very short supply, which you can improve by making prayer G which requires researching more technologies H, I and J... and it goes on and on and on.

The game also hates you. You absolutely require note-taking capabilities, or just ruin the intent of the game (discovery and experimentation) by using the wiki. The game does the bare minimum to help you manage recipes, knowledge, inventory, quests...

You're meant to experiment to discover alchemy recipes, however the game does notthing to help you. It won't log failed combinations. It won't tell you what type of powder, liquid, or essence an item can be turned into, only that it'll turn into powder and/or liquid and/or essence. But get this, it also doesn't tell you that the item N you need for quest L is actually made using three components, which requires an entire new tier of alchemy apparatus, which in turns requires an entire new tier of furnance...

Each area you can build in has its own set of available constructions, but to find out what you need to bring with you, you have to go there first, then make a note of what's needed, travel back, grab the parts, head back, actually build it. And that's assuming that one of the parts is locked behind a technology in a completely different tech tree with no warning because the tech tree itself provides no information on the items you can unlock.

And then you actually make a step towards progression, hand in the item to the NPC, and all that happens is the next crafting/grinding step is revealed to you. And at no point does the game provide you with any UI to track and manage things.

And then after upgrading your church, you can't run any sermons, the game doesn't tell you, and you're left stuck with no faith to progress with until you resort to searching the web to discover that while the Bishop has no quest listed to get some papers, you need to get some papers (which cost money, so off you go grinding some more to get money first) and hand them to the Bishop to continue doing the weekly sermons.

30 hours in, and while it was certainly a new experience, I'm left feeling like then next 30 hours are going to be just as grindy as the first 30, and I'll maybe finish off four more quests... maybe...

TLDR: The game is unfinished and should be in early access. As it currently is, I can not recommend the game.

I rarely give games negative ratings because usually I can see that I do not like a game long before I have played enough to be able to review it properly. This is one of the exceptions where I love the concept of the game and felt like I wanted to keep playing but can not forgive it for its flaws.
This game targets a niche genre of games like Harvest Moon and more recently Stardew Valley. Those series have gameplay loops of taking care of crops, animals, foraging, building relationships, and managing the amount of work you perform per day. Graveyard Keeper has many of the same loops just in different forms. There are crops to grow, but there are also the main gimmick which is the corpses that you must prepare and bury in the titular graveyard. A fresh look on a genre that, while something I still enjoy, tends to stick to the tried and true farming lifestyle. 
To give credit where credit is due, Graveyard Keeper does have a lot of aesthetic and design choices that feel great. The art style is sprite based, but a higher resolution so it feels fresh. Unlocking abilities and tools behind a research mechanic gives the player sight of how many things they will eventually be able to do. Unlocking sleep from the standard day/night cycle helps those "I just have 1 more thing to do today!" feelings when you run out of time in other games. Even the limitations on what you can sell is interesting because you can't assume you can make money doing just anything.
However, that is about as far as I can go with the praise, as the more I played the less I enjoyed the game. I suffered from many performance issues from major stuttering to jerky character movement. This doesn't appear to be unique to me as I noticed more than one thread complaining about this with none of the proposed solutions helping me or the people in the thread. This being a sprite based 2-d game, it should not be difficult for it to run cleanly without any performance issues on computers even half the power of the one that I am running. There are also many issues with the pacing and direction the game gives in regards to the early tutorial and the quest/story chain as you play through the game. There are clearly unfinished parts or instructions the game gives you that are not actually true in the game engine. Late game suffers from an obtuse alchemy system with far too many possible combinations for it to be reasonable to find without a wiki. Several of the final goals of the game revolve around obtaining a large amount of money which drags out the end of the game while not giving many forms of improvement.
I feel this game is a diamond in the rough, but without polishing it will not be worth the money asked for it. I have a list of concerns and complaints that, while not exhaustive, if addressed I would gladly change my review to something more positive. We will see if this game is ever deserving of it though.

1. Gameplay performance needs to be improved considerably. Stuttering is not acceptable in a game this graphically simplistic.
2. While I have only had a few bugs, there are a lot of reports of issues, so this should be addressed along with the rest of this list.
3. Early game quest chains need to be more informative to the player. You start off getting meat from a corpse but being able to do much with it is locked out until much later in the game. The graveyard should be able to be restored with just the repair kits given at the beginning, as repair kits are only unlocked much later.
4. Church upgrades should demand that the player get the appropriate citizen upgrade before letting them upgrade it. Locking players out of one of the better sources of early income is not good.
5. Fix the missing components. Advertising the crop shipping company does not improve the selling price, which is counter to what the merchant tells you in game. In addition the entire printing press research line is worthless because it only lets you create flyers that are not needed that late in the game. It is pretty obvious that these are remnants of cut content and need to be fixed.
6. Alchemy needs to have an alternate method of discovering potions. Right now you have to exhaustively mix each component with each other component to see what happens. There are far too many components and far too few recipies for this to make sense. Perhaps a system where you use the component to research it further and discovering which components work well with others could work here.
7. A lot of time is spent juggling lumber and shipping containers over large distances. This is not interesting gameplay and a simple solution would be to add carts or some way to use the donkey to haul goods and lumber.
8. Late game grinding for blue science and money is merely a waste of time. Grinding is a part of this genre, but there has to be something to make it worthwhile.
9. Movement is very slow in this game. A sprinting mechanism that burns energy might be a benefit. There is a speed potion, but that runs into the issues with alchemy so it isn't a solid fix.
10. The NPCs only being around during a certain day is interesting, but combined with the slow movement (even with the teleportation stone), there were several times where I missed interacting with the NPC. Overlapping NPC days would allow for the unique day to find them, but also give a little leeway in going to talk to them. Something as simple as them staying for two days each, or the entire day/night cycle on their day.
11. Blue science is far too difficult to get. It artificially locks the player out of advancing naturally. Blue science should be obtainable from regularly performed tasks related to either the autopsy system, or the alchemy system to encourage players to keep using those systems while also not relying on the player spending their hard earned money buying books once a week (I learned it was something I should be doing early on and I still had to buy books for long after I was done with the rest of the research points).

Definitely recommend. There are not many games like Graveyard Keeper, Stardew Valley or Traveller's Rest and this is the best of this kind.
